reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Ashcraft Pediatric Surgery
clinicalPearls: A congenital interruption of oesophageal continuity, most commonly with a distal fistula connecting the trachea to the lower oesophageal pouch
Presents at or soon after birth with frothing, drooling, choking, and cyanotic episodes with feeds, often after antenatal polyhydramnios
Inability to pass a nasogastric or orogastric tube into the stomach, with the tube coiling in the upper pouch on chest radiograph, is the classic diagnostic clue
Gas in the stomach and bowel indicates a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula, whereas a gasless abdomen suggests pure atresia without a distal fistula
The five anatomical patterns range from atresia with distal fistula (most common) to isolated atresia, isolated (H-type) fistula, and proximal fistula variants
Strongly linked to the VACTERL association, so vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, renal, and limb anomalies should be screened for
Management is surgical repair with ligation of any fistula and oesophageal anastomosis, primarily or in stages when the gap is long
reference.pathophysiology: Oesophageal atresia with or without tracheo-oesophageal fistula results from abnormal separation of the primitive foregut into the trachea and oesophagus during early gestation, when the tracheoesophageal septum normally divides the two structures. Faulty septation leaves the oesophagus discontinuous and frequently maintains an abnormal communication between the airway and oesophagus. A distal fistula allows air to enter the stomach and permits reflux of gastric contents into the lungs, while secretions pooling in the blind upper pouch spill into the trachea, both contributing to aspiration and respiratory compromise. Associated tracheomalacia and dysmotility of the repaired oesophagus are common longer-term issues.
additionalDifferentials: Duodenal atresia (as a coexisting anomaly rather than mimic)
additionalInvestigations: Attempted passage of a radio-opaque orogastric tube with chest radiograph showing coiling in the upper pouch
Chest and abdominal radiograph to assess distal bowel gas indicating a fistula
Echocardiography to define cardiac anatomy and the side of the aortic arch before surgery
Renal and spinal ultrasound and vertebral/limb assessment for VACTERL screening
Bronchoscopy to localise a fistula, including an H-type or proximal fistula
Contrast study (carefully performed) when an isolated H-type fistula is suspected
redFlags: Recurrent cyanotic and choking episodes with aspiration before repair
Marked gaseous abdominal distension from a large distal fistula worsening ventilation
Coexisting major congenital heart disease affecting operative risk
Respiratory failure requiring ventilation, which can force fistula gas into the stomach
Anastomotic leak, stricture, or recurrent fistula after repair
reference.prognosis: Survival is excellent for infants without severe cardiac or chromosomal anomalies, and most achieve satisfactory swallowing. Long-gap atresia, major associated anomalies, and prematurity worsen outcomes, and many children have ongoing reflux, oesophageal strictures, dysmotility, or tracheomalacia requiring follow-up.
pitfalls: Feeding a drooling neonate before excluding oesophageal atresia
Missing an isolated H-type fistula, which can present later with recurrent chest infections
Overlooking the VACTERL association and undetected cardiac or renal anomalies
Failing to identify a right-sided aortic arch, which alters the surgical approach
Attributing all postoperative feeding problems to stricture without considering dysmotility or recurrent fistula
management: Preoperative stabilisation with continuous suction of the upper pouch via a Replogle tube, head-up positioning and withholding oral feeds to prevent aspiration
Surgical repair with division and ligation of the tracheo-oesophageal fistula and primary oesophageal anastomosis, using staged or delayed repair for long-gap atresia
Echocardiography and screening for VACTERL-associated vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, renal and limb anomalies before surgery
Postoperative respiratory support with management of anastomotic leak, stricture and tracheomalacia
Long-term treatment of gastro-oesophageal reflux with acid suppression (proton-pump inhibitors) and endoscopic dilatation of strictures for the associated dysmotility
Multidisciplinary follow-up across paediatric surgery, respiratory medicine, gastroenterology and feeding or nutrition services
